content.prompt: The distance from Adelaide to Uluru is $1550\text{ km}$, and the distance from Adelaide to Darwin via Uluru is $3050\text{ km}$. How far is Uluru from Darwin?

Subtract the Adelaide–Uluru distance from the total distance via Uluru.

Trade one thousand for ten hundreds: $10-5=5$ hundreds and $2-1=1$ thousand. Uluru is $1500\text{ km}$ from Darwin.

content.prompt: Jacqui is 183 cm tall, David is 152 cm tall and Adrian is 147 cm tall. How much taller than each of the others is Jacqui?

answer.short: Jacqui is 31 cm taller than David and 36 cm taller than Adrian.
answer.worked:
Compared with David:
$$183-152=31\text{ cm}.$$
Compared with Adrian, trade one ten in 183 to give 7 tens and 13 ones:
$$\begin{align*}183-147&=100+70+13-(100+40+7)\\183-147&=36\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
Jacqui is 31 cm taller than David and 36 cm taller than Adrian.

teachingContext.methodNote: Subtract each shorter height from Jacqui's height. The supplied Chapter 1 page 10 teaches trading or decomposition for subtraction requiring regrouping.

content.prompt: A hotel has 17 rooms on each floor. If the hotel consists of three buildings, each with 27 floors, how many rooms are there in the hotel?

answer.worked:
There are $3\times27=81$ floors altogether.

$$\begin{align*}81\times17&=81\times(10+7)\\81\times17&=810+567\\81\times17&=1377\end{align*}$$

The hotel has 1377 rooms.

answer.short:
Sample answers: $2$, $3$ and $8$.

Their squares and cubes have no digits in common.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2^2&=2\times2=4\\2^3&=2\times2\times2=8\\3^2&=3\times3=9\\3^3&=3\times3\times3=27\\8^2&=8\times8=64\\8^3&=8\times8\times8=512\end{align*}$$

The pairs $4$ and $8$, $9$ and $27$, and $64$ and $512$ each have no digits in common. Thus $2$, $3$ and $8$ satisfy the condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the earliest common ringing time for four fractional intervals by expressing them in a common time unit and finding their least common multiple.

content.prompt: Four bells start tolling together and ring every $1$, $1\frac{1}{4}$, $1\frac{1}{5}$ and $1\frac{1}{6}$ seconds, respectively. After what period of time will they first ring all together again?

answer.short:
210 seconds.

Express the intervals in a common time unit and find their least common multiple.
answer.worked:
In units of $\frac{1}{60}$ second, the four intervals are:
$$\begin{align*}1&=\frac{60}{60}\\1\frac{1}{4}&=\frac{75}{60}\\1\frac{1}{5}&=\frac{72}{60}\\1\frac{1}{6}&=\frac{70}{60}\end{align*}$$
Find the least common multiple by listing multiples.
The first common multiple of $60$ and $75$ is $300$. Their common multiples are $300,600,900,1200,1500,1800,\ldots$; the first divisible by $72$ is $1800$.
Common multiples of $60$, $75$ and $72$ are therefore $1800,3600,5400,7200,9000,10800,12600,\ldots$. The first divisible by $70$ is $12600$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Time}&=12600\div60\\&=210\text{ seconds}\end{align*}$$

An odd sum requires one even number and one odd number. Their product has an even factor, so it is even, including when the even number is zero.

inlines.text: An algorithm for changing base is shown below.
The number in the previous example is used to illustrate this.
remainder 3
remainder 1

The remainders, in reverse order, give the base 4 number (

answer.short: Each division by 4 gives the next digit, starting with the units digit. The quotient contains the remaining higher place values, so reading the remainders backwards gives $213_4$.
answer.worked:
Dividing by 4 separates the units remainder from groups of 4. Dividing the quotient again separates groups of 4 from groups of $4^2$:
$$\begin{align*}39&=4\times9+3\\9&=4\times2+1\\2&=4\times0+2.\end{align*}$$
Substituting the quotients back gives
$$\begin{align*}39&=4(4\times2+1)+3\\39&=2\times4^2+1\times4+3\\39_{10}&=213_4.\end{align*}$$
The remainders are found from the lowest place value upwards, so reversing their order puts the digits in the usual highest-to-lowest place-value order.

entries.description:
Choose any whole number to start with.
If it is odd, multiply it by 3 and then add 1.
If it is even, divide it by 2.
Then repeat this process on the number just obtained. Keep repeating the procedure.
For example, if you start with 58, the resulting chain of numbers is:
58, 29, 88, 44, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 1, …
The Collatz conjecture, made by Lothar Collatz in 1937, claims that, if you repeat this process over and over, starting with any whole number greater than zero, eventually you will finish up with the sequence … 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 1.
A conjecture is a statement that is thought to be true but has not been proved mathematically to be true for all cases. Although the Collatz conjecture has been shown to work — often very quickly — for many whole numbers, there are some quite small numbers that take a very long time to come down to … 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 1.
Apply this process to all the whole numbers greater than zero and less than or equal to 30. For each one, find:
• how many steps it takes to reach 1 the first time
• the largest number in the sequence. (For the sequence above, 58 takes 19 steps and reaches a maximum of 88.)
Look for shortcuts and work with a partner if you like.

entries.description:
First note that 4² = 16 and 4³ = 64.
There are two lots of 16 in 39, as 2 × 16 = 32. This leaves 7, which is one lot of 4 and three lots of 1.
39 = 2 × 4² + 1 × 4 + 3
We can write 39 (base 10) = 213 (base 4) or 39₁₀ = 213₄.
This is read as ‘three nine base 10 is equal to two one three, base 4’.
